Question: Is the infinite monkey theorem actually possible?
Answer: There is a theorem in mathematics that has been called the infinite monkey theorem. Here’s a special case of it. Suppose that an infinite sequence of letters is randomly written from an alphabet of 26 letters. Then every finite string made from those letters will appear with probability 1. For example, the string “thequickbrownfoxjumpsoverthelazydog” will appear somewhere with probability 1. It’s 35 letters long, so don’t expect it to occur soon. You may have to wait until about the 26 35 place to find it. If you get hoard of monkeys typing randomly, they’ll all die before they type that string. It’s a real theorem in mathematics with a real proof. But it doesn’t apply to actual monkeys with finite lifespans.

Question: It has been proven that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH) cannot be proven true or false using the axioms of ZFC. But it must actually be true or false because either there is a set of Reals with cardinality between N and R or there isn't. Am I wrong?

Question: How does Euclid's definition of equivalent ratios relate to our modern understanding of equivalent ratios?
Answer: It’s the same, at least for ratios of positive magnitudes. The fifth book of Euclid’s Elements includes the research of Eudoxus a generation or two before Euclid. It says that two ratios of positive magnitudes are equal if they compare the same way to ratios of positive integers. A ratio a / b of positive magnitudes is equal to another ratio c / d when they compare the same way to all ratios m / n of positive integers. Dedekind used this to define a real number as what we now call a Dedekind cut of rational numbers. For Dedekind, a real number is something that separates rational numbers m / n into two nonempty sets, the elements of one subset (the left subset) being less than or equal to all the elements of the other subset (the right subset). There are two distinctions between Eudoxus’ concept and Dedekind’s concept. First, Eudoxus only considered positive magnitudes and positive ratios while Dedekind allowed for ratios to be zero or negative. The second is that Eudoxus required magnitudes to define ratios, but Dedekind’s concept was more abstract so didn’t require preexisting magnitudes for real numbers.

Question: How do we define numbers we cannot count up to?
Answer: There are lots of numbers that are defined without using counting. For example, the cube root of 5 is that number whose cube is 5. You may be asking, however, about natural numbers, 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 … . Children learn numbers by counting, often counting on their fingers. That gets them up to ten. By the time they’ve done that, they’ve heard that there are larger numbers—eleven, twelve, and so forth. They can learn them as well, but no longer just using their fingers. At some point, counting doesn’t do it. People just don’t have the time to keep counting. For a long time, we’ve has Indo-Arabic numerals. You can determine a number like 92,384,529,843,765 just by giving its decimal representation. That’s pretty neat. For most purposes, that’s good enough. But there are numbers so large that it’s impractical to use decimal representation. There are lots of other ways to identify them. One of the first to do that was Ackermann. He wasn’t interested in numbers so much as in functions and algorithms. There is a way to create rapidly growing functions by iterating already known functions. It’s called induction. For example, multiplication is repeated addition, and exponentiation is repeated multiplication, and hyperexponentiation is repeated exponentiation. Ackermann collected these all into one grand operation, see Ackermann function - Wikipedia. Anyway, the numbers defined by Ackermann’s function are so huge that there’s no way to count up to them even though they’re clearly defined by the function.

Question: Which, if any, of the axioms of ZF Set Theory are considered "constructive"?
Answer: “Constructive” is not a precise term, but all the axioms of ZF except regularity are constructive in the intuitive sense of that word. Let’s review the axioms. The only ones that could be nonconstructive are those that say something exists without saying what it is. Most of them don’t say something exists, so we can pass by them. The axiom of regularity (also called the axiom of foundation) says Every non-empty set contains a element disjoint from it. That’s nonconstructive. It says if S is a set, then there is an element x ∈ S such that there is no element y ∈ S that is also an element of x . It’s not a particularly important axiom, and non-wellfounded set theory doesn’t need it. Some of the other axioms of ZF aren’t constructive, but they’re usually stated that way because the rest of the axioms imply a constructive version of them. For example, the axiom of union says that there is a set that contains all the elements of given sets. The rest of the axioms imply there is a unique set that contains all the elements of the given sets and no other elements, called the union of those sets. Likewise, the axiom of infinite says there’s some infinite set, but you can use the rest of the axioms to prove that the set of Von Neumann natural numbers N is an infinite set. The axiom of choice (AC), however, is not constructive. It’s not an axiom of ZF, but an axiom of ZFC, which means Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with AC included.

Question: If "some x are y", does that mean that "some y are x"? If so, is there a related rule of inference?

The words “also” and “and” signify conjunction, and conjunction is commutative. P z ∧ Q z is true exactly when Q z ∧ P z is true. Commutativity of conjunction holds in all logical systems. Question: Is mathematics causal? Or violation of causality?

Question: What are the axioms of the projective plane?

The third axiom is needed to exclude projective lines as being projective planes. From these axioms you can prove the theorem that there are four lines that do not pass through the same point (which is the dual of the third axiom). There are many different projective planes. One is the real projective plane. Another is the finite projective plane that has 13 points and 13 lines. It’s based on the finite field of three elements. For each field, like R and Z 3 , there is a corresponding projective plane. There are some projective planes, however, that aren’t based on fields.

Question: Why is the reflexive property of congruence not stated explicitly as an axiom while transitivity is?
Answer: An equivalence relation on sets is always defined as a binary relation that’s reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Reflexivity is required since the empty relation is symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive. Congruence relations are equivalence relations that are compatible with operations you are considering. For example, a congruence relation on an Abelian group has to satisfy x ≡ x + 0 x ≡ y  implies  − x ≡ − y x ≡ y  and  w ≡ z  imply  x + w ≡ y + z Reflexivity follows from x ≡ x + 0 = x , so it could be dropped as a requirement. I wouldn’t though since it makes more sense to start with congruence being a special kind of equivalence relation.

Question: Hi From the sixteenth century people have published mathematical series that they wrote 'equals pi'. Since they did not know the precise value for pi, on what argument were they able to state that their series = pi?

Question: In set theory, we consider lengths as an infinite set of points and we can prove that all lengths have a one to one correspondence of points. Does that mean all lengths are equal?

Question: According to Euchid division, remainders are strictly non-negative. So, if I have 2n-1 and divide it by 2, I get, n with -1 remainder. In math only (not CS), should it be n-1 with 1 remainder?

Question: What is the following problem called? How are finite amount of points in n dimensional euclidian space distributed so that they are equidistant to their centroid. Equivalently: When is the centroid of points on a sphere the center of the sphere?

(It’s enough to check the squares of those distances are the same.) For example, take four points in the plane ( x 1 , y 1 ) , ( x 2 , y 2 ) , ( x 3 , y 3 ) , and ( x 4 , y 4 ) . Their centroid is ( ¯¯¯ x , ¯¯¯ y ) = ( 1 4 ( x 1 + x 2 + x 3 + x 4 ) , 1 4 ( y 1 + y 2 + y 3 + y 4 ) ) . The four points are equidistant from the centroid if ( x i − ¯¯¯ x ) 2 + ( y i − ¯¯¯ y ) 2 has the same value for i = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4. A particular example of that is the four vertices of a rectangle whose center is the origin.

Question: Can I invent axioms and logic models? It does not have to have anything to do with the universe; it is enough if it is consistent within itself. Is it an absolute fact that I can invent axioms and logical models? Or is it a matter of opinion?
Answer: It’s not so much axioms that you invent, but theories that have axioms as their basis. A theory has a language, that is, terms that can be used in statements. A theory also has specific axioms which are specified statements in that language. A model of that theory is anything which satisfies the axioms, that is, they’re true in that model. It follows that any statement that logically follows from the axioms (such statements are called theorems in the theory) will also be true in the model. Can you invent such a thing? Sure. Why not? If you like you can start with something that will eventually be a model of the theory. Then choose some statements to be axioms for the theory. An advantage of that is you know that the theory you construct is consistent. One model is enough to imply consistency. Example. Suppose you’re interested in constructing a theory of subtraction. (I know it’s been done before, but this is an example.) The language consists of only a binary operation you call subtraction and denote in the usual way. Given two things a and b , then there is another thing denoted a − b which is determined by a and b . Now you get to select some axioms for subtraction. Which axioms you choose are up to you, and different theories can result from which axioms you choose. For example, you might take an axiom that says there is something, which you’ll denote 0, with the property that when you subtract it from anything, the result is that thing. Symbolically, for each a it is the case that a − 0 = a . There are lots of other axioms you could take like ( a − b ) − c = ( a − c ) − b . You probably had as a model for this theory the usual subtraction operation on numbers, but what other models are there? There’s a good chance that the axioms you chose also hold for a binary operation on two elements, 0 and 1, where 0 − 0 = 0 , 1 − 0 = 1 , 0 − 1 = 1 , and 1 − 1 = 0. If so, that’s another model for the theory.

Question: What is the fundamental group of R^2 — {a, b} and R^3 — {a,b}?
Answer: You’re asking for the fundamental group of the plane minus two points, and the fundamental group of 3-space minus two points. The plane minus two points is the free group generated by two elements where one element describes going around one point, and the other going around the other point. More generally, when you remove n points from the plane, the fundamental group is the free group on n elements. When n = 1 , you get the free group generated by one element, and that’s the familiar infinite cyclic group. Space is very different. Every closed curve can be contracted to a point even when you specify the contractions must not pass through a finite number of points. So the fundamental group is trivial.

Question: Prove the identity 7(x-8)-3 (x-20) =4(x+1). Do I need to prove l.h.s=r.h.s or Is it compulsory to check it for random values of x to prove its identity or not?
Answer: To show an equation is an identity, you need to prove that it’s true for all values of the variable, not just for one random value. Here’s an equation that’s not an identity even though it’s true for one value of the variable: x 2 − 5 = x + 1 . You can check that it’s true for x = 3 , but it’s not an identity since it’s not true for all values of x . A typical way of proving an equation is an identity is to reduce it to simpler forms by reversible steps. For 7 ( x − 8 ) − 3 ( x − 20 ) = 4 ( x + 1 ) you can simplify the terms. Simplifying is reversible. 7 x − 56 − 3 x + 60 = 4 x + 4 4 x + 4 = 4 x + 4 Since both sides are equal, that’s true for all values of x . Therefore your equation is an identity. Other reversible steps include adding something to both sides of the equation, and subtracting something from both sides of the equation. Also, multiplying multiplying and dividing both sides by a nonzero number. Squaring both sides of an equation is not reversible. So when you do that, you might introduce extraneous solutions. For example, the equation x − 3 = 1 has only the solution x = 4 , but ( x − 3 ) 2 = 1 also has the solution x = 2 , which is an extraneous solution of the original equation. So whenever you square both sides of an equation, you have to check which of the new solutions of the new equation were solutions of the original equation.

Question: Is it true that the Pythagoreans believed that all numbers were rational, that is either integers or fractions?
Answer: The word they used for number means what we call positive integer: 1, 2, 3, and so forth. They also had magnitudes which included things like line segments, plane figures, and solids. It seems that they expected any two magnitudes of the same type, like two line segments, to be commensurable, that is, they expected there to be a shorter line segment that exactly measured both line segments. So if the first line segment is 3 times the short one, and the second is 5 times the short one, then the ratio of the first to the second is 3 to 5. We would say the ratio is the rational number 3/5. Early on, they discovered that there are line segments that don’t have a common measure. In particular, the diagonal d of a square and its side s are not commensurable. There is no short line segment that exactly measures both d and s . So they couldn’t explain what the ratio d to s is. (We call it √ 2 . ) This led to the question: what is the ratio of two magnitudes of the same type if it’s not the ratio of two numbers? That’s an interesting question. About a century and a half later, Eudoxus (390–340 BC) found a way to express ratios of magnitudes in terms of ratios of numbers. It’s essentially what Dedekind used to define real numbers, now called Dedekind cuts.

Question: Can every real number be expressed, to whatever degree of accuracy desired, as a subset (collection) of the natural numbers, if the subset (collection) allows for repeating particular natural numbers?

So, for example, if your real number starts off with 0.707106 … you would include the natural numbers 1 + 7 = 8 , 2 + 7 + 0 = 9 , 3 + 7 + 0 + 7 = 17 , 4 + 7 + 0 + 7 + 1 = 19 , and so forth. You could modify that encoding to take care of other real numbers. The idea is that there are enough subsets of natural numbers to construct an injective function from the real numbers to the set of subsets of natural numbers.

Question: How can you show that there are only 6 different trees on 6 vertices?

You've got a linear subtree with 5 vertices, and 1 more vertex to attach to it. It could attach to the middle vertex, or to a vertex next to the middle vertex. That’s all there are of this kind. Consider next trees of diameter 4. You need to attach two vertices to a linear subtree of 4 vertices. They could both attach to the same non-leaf vertex or to different non-leaf vertices. There are two of this kind. Of trees of diameter 3, there is only one way to attach the other 3 vertices, and that’s to the middle vertex. That’s all 6 of them.

Question: Does the definition of a perfect number necessitate that it is even?

In Book IX, proposition 36, he gave a construction for some even perfect numbers. In modern notation, it says that if 2 p − 1 is a prime number, then ( 2 p − 1 ) 2 p − 1 is a perfect number. Euclid didn’t claim that every perfect number is of that form, and he didn’t even claim that every even perfect number was of that form. They’ve been studied a lot since Euclid’s time. Question: Why are ascending sequences permitted in set theory (ZFC), when infinite descending sequences are forbidden?
Answer: I think you’re asking why set theory allows an infinite sequence of sets each is contained in the next (i.e., each is a member of the next) S 0 ∈ S 1 ∈ S 2 ∈ ⋯ ∈ S n ∈ ⋯ but not an infinite sequence of sets where each contains the next S 0 ∋ S 1 ∋ S 2 ∋ ⋯ ∋ S n ∋ ⋯ . The axiom of regularity implies there aren’t any descending sequences like that. It also implies no set can be a member of itself, and a few other things. So your question becomes: Why do we have the axiom of regularity? It wasn’t in Zermelo’s original set theory. Von Neumann proposed adding something equivalent to it in 1925, and Zermelo included the axiom of regularity in his 1930 textbook on set theory. Most of mathematics doesn’t depend on the axiom of regularity. The axiom of regularity implies that every set has an ordinal rank, a measure of the complexity of a set. The ordinal rank of a set defined as the smallest ordinal greater than all the ordinal ranks of its elements. The axiom of regularity also allows what’s called ϵ -induction on sets. That says that one way you can prove a property holds for all sets is just to show an inductive step: if the property holds for every element of a set, then it holds for the set itself. If you can prove that inductive step, then it holds for all sets. (If there are infinite descending sequences of sets, then ϵ -induction doesn’t work.) With ϵ -induction, things like properties of ordinal numbers are easier to prove. For some kinds of set theory, like non-wellfounded set theory, the axiom of regularity is not included.

Question: Could a regular hexagon tiling be considered a platonic solid?
Answer: No, but it’s just as interesting. You can think of planar tilings (including the hexagonal one) and Platonic solids as belonging to one larger family of tessellations, or tilings. Schläfli introduced symbols {n,k} to describe these tilings. An {n,k}-tiling has regular n-gons meeting k at a time at each vertex. There are three tilings of the Euclidean plane: {3,6} in which equilateral triangles meet six at each vertex; {4,4} in which squares meet four at each vertex; and {6,3} in which hexagons meet three at each vertex. You can interpret the Platonic solids as tilings of an elliptic plane, that is, a sphere. There are five of them: icosahedron {3,5}, octahedron {3,4}, tetrahedron {3,3}, cube {4,3}, and dodecahedron {5,3}. There are also infinitely many tilings of a hyperbolic plane. You can determine whether {n,k} will be a tessellation of the Euclidean plane, the hyperbolic plane, or the elliptic plane by looking at the sum 1/n + 1/k. If the sum equals 1/2, as it does for the three tessellations mentioned above, then {n,k} is a Euclidean tessellation. If the sum is less than 1/2, then the tessellation is hyperbolic; but if greater than 1/2, then elliptic. Here’s a {5,4} tiling of the hyperbolic plane shown in a Poincaré disk model of that plane. See Hyperbolic Tessellations for more about hyperbolic tilings, a page I put on the web in 1994.

Answer: Apeirogons are polygons. A circle is not a polygon. A circle consists of all the points at a given distance, the radius, from a given point, the center. It is a curve and it has the property that for any two points on it, the line through those two points does not have any other points that lie on that circle. No polygon has those properties. An apeirogon is usually defined as a regular infinite sided polygon. It has many straight line segments of the same length as its sides. There are no regular apeirogons in a Euclidean plane, but they do exist in hyperbolic planes. If you don’t require regularity, that is, the sides don’t all have to have the same length, then there are such things in Euclidean geometry.

Question: How can I tell looking at a pedigree family tree (genealogy) if the disease is autosomal dominant/recessive or X-linked dominant/REcessive?
Answer: Let’s look at the four cases: (1) dominant and not X linked, (2) dominant and X linked, (3) recessive and not X linked, and (4) recessive and X linked. Assume also that the trait is evident when it occurs, that is, you can easily tell when an individual has sit. Dominant and not X linked. In order for a child to get it, at least one parent has to have it. If exactly one parent has it, the probability of the child getting it is 1/2 (or greater). If both parents have it, the probability of the child getting it is 3/4 (or greater). (The greater occurs when a parent has two copies of the gene for the disease.) Dominant and X linked. As before, in order for a child to receive it, at least one parent has to have it. When the father has it and not the mother, then all of his daughters will get it but none of his sons. When the mother has it and not the father, then the probability of the child getting it is 1/2 (or greater). When both parents have it, the daughters will get it, and the sons will get it with probability 1/2. Recessive and not X linked. If either parent doesn’t have it and is not a carrier (which you may not know), the child won’t get it. If both parents are carriers (which you may not know), the child will get it with probability 1/4. If one parent has it and the other is a carrier, the child will get it with probability 1/2. If both have it, the child will get it. Recessive and X linked. If it’s X linked, the father either has it or not. There’s no possibility of just a carrier for him. So the child get it if the father doesn’t have it, but if the father does, then the child will at least be a carrier and the rest depends on the mother. If the father has it, there are three subcases. If the mother has it, the child will get it. If the mother is a carrier, then the child will get it with probability 1/2. Otherwise, the child won’t get it. Most traits aren’t simply dominant or recessive, and they’re often determined by combinations of genes, so things are usually much messier than described above.

Question: What will happen if a non-academic mathematician proves such a big conjecture in math, like odd perfect numbers or something?
Answer: The real problem with explanations written by someone who isn’t experienced with mathematics is that it’s hard to understand what they’re saying. I know that from reading lots of it from people who sent me proofs and from what I’ve read here on Quora and elsewhere. They don’t use standard terminology and notation, and sometimes when they do, they misuse it. They introduce new terms that aren’t clearly defined. It takes a lot to figure out just what is meant. In the case of odd perfect numbers, at least the terminology is clear. The prime factorization theorem will be understood by the author, and the author will probably use the divisor function σ ( n ) (sum of the positive divisors of n ) properly. So at least the start of an explanation of a proof solving the odd-perfect-number conjecture would be understandable. What this all means is that when a journal receives an article that doesn’t use standard terminology, has poorly defined new terms, and is otherwise hard to comprehend, the editor will reject it without even sending it to reviewers.

Question: Are there also false statements that cannot be proved -- according to Godel's First incompleteness Theorem?
Answer: Every statement that’s false in a model of a theory cannot be proved in that theory. If you’re talking about proofs, you’ve got some theory in mind with axioms. If you’re talking about truth values, you’ve got some model of that theory in mind. That means all the axioms of the theory are true for the model. It follows that every statement you can prove from the axioms (that is, all the theorems in the theory) are true for the model. (Logical deductions preserve truth, so if the axioms are true in the model, so all the theorems are true in the model. As an implication that last sentence says: If a statement can be proved in a theory, it’s true in every model. The contrapositive of that says: If a statement is false in a model, it can’t be proved in the theory. Note that this doesn’t have anything to do with Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem.

Question: How far can we go with pure Euclidean geometry as opposed to analytical geometry?
Answer: Synthetic geometry is what Euclid did. Axioms, definitions, and theorems with proofs that only use deductive logic. Analytic geometry uses coordinates that Fermat and Descartes developed in the early 1600s. The main advantage of analytic geometry is that the basic terms of geometry—points, lines, curves, angles, length, and area—can be described and analyzed in terms of symbolic algebra. A plane curve, for example, corresponds to an equation in two variables. Finding where two curves intersect is reduced to solving two equations in those two variables. In the late 1600s calculus was developed. Newton proved his theorems on calculus by synthetic geometry because at that time algebra was new and its only theoretical basis came from geometry. I suppose that anything that can be done with analytic geometry could still be done with synthetic geometry. The proofs, however, would be more complex. Apollonius of Perga (a century after Euclid)[1] developed the theory of conic sections—parabolas, hyperbolas, and ellipses—completely with synthetic geometry. It’s hard to follow what he did because it’s so complex. Most everything about conic sections reduces to analyzing quadratic equations in two variables. That’s so much simpler with analytic geometry. Question: Gravity is what pushes us down. How does it "act" at the center of the Earth?
Answer: As you do down towards the center of the Earth, first the force of gravity increases, then it decreases to zero at the center. If the Earth had constant density everywhere within it, then the force of gravity would be proportional to the distance to the center of the Earth. Half way to the center of the earth you would weigh half as much. But the earth doesn’t have constant density. The mantle is much less dense than the core, so much less dense that the force of gravity increases as you go down through the mantle. Then as you continue going down through the core, the force of gravity deceases almost linearly, and it’s down to zero at the center of the Earth. There’s something called the Preliminary Reference Earth Model[1] that predicts what the force of gravity is in terms of the distance to the center of the Earth. Note that beyond the radius of the Earth, gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance to the center of the earth. (The curve on the right is part of a hyperbola.)

Question: How do I actually study mathematics? I like it but I barely know what to do other than just rewrite formulas over and over again.
Answer: Here are some suggestions. Familiarity with terminology and notation Unless you know what the words and symbols mean, you’ll be stuck. Terminology is given by definitions, and many of the words in the definitions are defined in earlier definitions. Be sure you know what they mean. Special notations are often included in the definitions. For example, here’s the definition of “divides” as used in number theory. Definition. An integer m is said to divide an integer n when there is another integer k such that k m = n . When m divides n , that’s denoted as m ∣ n . When m doesn’t divide n , that’s denoted as m ∤ n . You’ll find commentary and examples after the definition. You might see something that says another way to express m ∣ n is to say the quotient n / m is an integer. Examples could include 6 ∣ 30 and 4 ∤ 30. To become familiar with the terminology and notation, use it in exercises given in textbooks, that is, solve some math problems. Understand the reasoning behind mathematical facts A statement in mathematics that is shown by deductive logic to hold is called a theorem, and that reasoning using deductive logic is the proof of the theorem. Try to understand that reasoning. Sometimes the reasoning isn’t a complete logical proof, but it’s convincing nonetheless. For example, take a common illustration the multiplication of positive integers is commutative, that is, m times n is equal to n times m . That’s often illustrated by taking a specific case, say 3 times 4, then drawing 12 dots in 3 rows and 4 columns. You’ll get the same 12 dots if you turn your head sideways to see 4 rows and 3 columns. That’s pretty convincing, but it doesn’t use deductive logic. Whether you use strict deductive logic or some other convincing argument, you should know why mathematical statements and formulas hold. Learn how to make these arguments yourself. For example, you should be able to come up with proofs for the following statements: If m ∣ n and m ∣ k , then m ∣ ( n + k ) . If m ∣ n and n ∣ k , then m ∣ k . As you progress in mathematics, you’ll find proofs become more and more important.

Question: Is the fractal Sierspinki cube also known as a Menger cube in fact a paradox since as iterations approach infinity the volume approaches 0, while the surface area approaches infinity?

Question: What is the physical example of an abelian group?
Answer: Consider a merry-go-round (carousel), and consider its rotations. It can rotate by one angle, say 30°, and it can rotate by another angle, say 45°. Those two rotations could be performed one after the other (in either order) to get a 75° rotation. That composition of rotations is the binary operation of the Abelian group. There’s a special rotation, the one by 0°, that when composed with any other rotation results in that very other rotation. It’s the identity of the group. There are also inverse rotations. The inverse of a 45° rotation is –45° rotation, the one in the opposite direction. All those rotations form an Abelian group.

Question:

admit a vector space structure over the field of complex numbers?
Answer: Yes. When you say the Abelian group R under addition, you are not including the multiplication operation at all, just addition and subtraction. Call it G because it’s only a group, not a vector space, ring, or field. This Abelian group G is isomorphic a direct sum of an uncountable number of copies of the Abelian group Q . That, too, is a group, not a vector space, ring, or field, so call it H . So G ≅ ⨁ i ∈ I H where I is an uncountable set. Since an uncountable set I is the disjoint union of two uncountable sets I 1 ∪ I 2 , therefore ⨁ i ∈ I H ≅ ( ⨁ i ∈ I 1 H ) ⊕ ( ⨁ i ∈ I 2 H ) . That implies G ≅ G ⊕ G In other words, the Abelian group R is isomorphic to the Abelian group R 2 . But the Abelian group R 2 is isomorphic to the Abelian group C . Since, of course, C is a vector space over the field C , therefore the Abelian group R can be given a complex scalar multiplication to make it a complex vector space. Note that an uncountable set I is the disjoint union of any number of uncountable sets so long as that number is less than or equal to c , the cardinality of the real numbers. There, the Abelian group R can be given a complex scalar multiplication to make it a complex vector space C 2 , C 3 , … up to C c .

Question: How can there be any length to a line that is made up of points that have zero dimension? I haven't been able to find a good answer that intuitively make sense. Many people answer with mathematics that I'm not familiar with, like topology.
Answer: The expression “made up of” leaves a lot of room for interpretation. I’ll try to give an answer that may answer your question. Take a line ℓ . Fix a point P not on that line. Consider lines through point P that cross line ℓ . Each one of those intersect ℓ at a point that has dimension zero. There are infinitely many lines through P that cross ℓ , so there are infinitely many points on ℓ where they cross. Conversely, every point on ℓ is the intersection of a line through P that crosses ℓ at that point. Now, is there anything else to the line ℓ besides all those points on it? If you say no, then, then you’re good with the idea that the points make up the line. If you say yes, then you’ll have to say what else is needed to make up the line. You also ask about the length of a line segment. The length of a line is the same as the distance between its endpoints, and the distance between points doesn’t depend on the material between them. The length of a line segment is not the sum of the lengths of its points on it. However, if you cut a line segment into two line segments, then the the length of the whole line segment is the sum of the lengths of the two line segments.

Question: How do you generate any row of Pascal’s triangle? I need a general formula that can be used to generate any row by hand quickly. (can use classpad)
Answer: Take a number, say 10, and write these numbers down in a row. First write 1. Next divide that by 1 and multiply by 10 to get 10. Next divide that by 2 and multiply by 9 to get 45. Next divide that by 3 and multiply by 8 to get 120. Next divide that by 4 and multiply by 7 to get 210. Next divide that by 5 and multiply by 6 to get 252. Next divide that by 6 and multiply by 5 to get 210. You can keep doing this, but you can see the rest of the numbers are just going to be the previous ones in reverse order. 1 10 45 120 210 252 210 120 45 10 1 That’s the tenth row of the triangle. That process works for every row. It’s a standard algorithm. I learned it in my high school algebra class in the 1960s.

Question: How can something abstract be discovered? Platonists argue that mathematics is an abstract entity independent of the universe and that mathematics is discovery. Does this make sense? If we think like the Platonists, is God something discoverable?
Answer: In order to discover God by means of mathematics, you’ll have to have a language to describe what God is, and you’ll have to have some axioms expressed in that language. You’ll have to have enough of a theory to distinguish God from other things, or else whatever you proof applies to those other things as well. And your axioms? You can’t just have an axiom like “God exists”. Sure, you can, but the only people who accept that axiom as something of worth are those who already believe God exists. You need axioms that everyone can accept. If you can find those, and a proof from them that God exists, then maybe you’ve discovered God through mathematics. (When you’re a mathematician, it doesn’t matter if you think like a Platonist. A theorem is a theorem no matter who proved it, a Platonist, a formalist, or someone who has never thought about the philosophy of mathematics at all. They all agree what deductive logic is. You can’t even tell what their philosophy is by looking at what they’ve proved.)

Question: If we can only understand 3 dimensions, 4 at the most, how is it possible to believe there are any more, and what does that actually say about our reality?
Answer: We perceive three spatial dimensions from our senses—touch, sight, and hearing. So we have a special connection to three dimensions. But that doesn’t mean we can only understand 3 dimensions. We just can’t do that based solely on our experience from our senses. We can use our reasoning. Back in the 1600s Fermat and Descartes developed coordinate systems for 2 and 3 dimensions. At that time, if anyone had a reason to do so, they could have used coordinate systems any finite number of dimensions—4 dimensions, 5 dimensions, 6 dimensions, there’s no limit. But there didn’t seem to be a need for it. In the 1800s linear algebra was developed. It works fine for any number of dimensions. It’s an extension of what Fermat and Descartes did. It was needed because it had uses in physics. Since it was first developed, it’s had uses in statistics, engineering, economics, and other sciences. We do understand higher dimensions without having to visualize them. What does this say about reality? It’s reality that says we can perceive three spatial dimensions, not the other way around. We can understand any number of dimensions.

Question: Who first suggested that a line is a set of points?
Answer: I don’t know. It wasn’t Euclid. Euclid wrote that two points determine a line, that is to say, given two points A and B, there is exactly one line on which they lie. Nowhere in the Elements is there anything to suggest a set of points. Sets aren’t really needed if you’re only talking about a finite number of things since you can just list them. For example, the set of divisors of the number 10 is the set { 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 } , but you could just say the divisors of 10 are 1, 2, 5, and 10. It gets more difficult when there are infinitely many things to name. Dedekind and Cantor developed the concept of sets in the last third of the 19th century, a concept that allows the sets to have infinitely many points. They treated sets as things, like other things in mathematics. So it wouldn’t be until that period that someone would say that line is a set of points. You would have to search the literature to find actual references that say that. You’ll often see phrasing like that now. A line in R × R can be defined as the set of solutions of an equation of the form A x + B y = C where A , B , and C are fixed numbers and not both A and B are zero. It works. Question: The first two pages of Apostol’s mathematical analysis textbook he lists the field and order axioms. In Tao’s and other sources these are proved. I am referring to associativity etc. How can one treat as an axiom and other as a theorem?
Answer: Axioms define what you’re talking about. The axioms for the real number field say it’s a complete ordered field. But axioms don’t imply anything exist. The two most common constructions for real numbers are (1) Dedekind cuts of the set of rational numbers and (2) Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Both of those constructions require proofs to show the thing constructed satisfies the axioms for real numbers. An important theorem for real numbers is that if you have two models (Dedekind cuts, Cauchy sequences, or something else), then there is a unique isomorphism between them. Once you have that, you never have to use anything about the real numbers except their axioms. That means you can start with the axioms to do calculus and mathematical analysis. Axioms define real numbers, but you need something else to show they exist. The constructions mentioned above do that. When I took an honors calculus course in 1969 at the University of Michigan, the professor Thomas Storer spent the first two months on set theory, natural numbers, rational numbers, and real numbers. Question: Why doesn't the fact that any number divided by zero is undefined make the algebra violate completeness?

Question: What are some examples of monotone maps between semilattices that are not algebraic homomorphisms?

A homomorphism between two join-semilattices preserves the partial order (i.e., is monotone) and preserves joins. We’re looking for a function that that preserves partial orders but not joins. Question: What is Z [X] / ((x-2) *(x-3)) isomorphic to?
Answer: Consider the natural ring homomorphism Z [ x ] / ( ( x − 2 ) ( x − 3 ) ) → Z [ x ] / ( x − 2 ) × Z [ x ] / ( x − 3 ) which sends a polynomial modulo ( x − 2 ) ( x − 3 ) to the same polynomial twice, one time modulo x − 2 and the other time modulo x − 3. It’s well-defined since if two polynomials are congruent modulo ( x − 2 ) ( x − 3 ) , then they’re also well congruent modulo x − 2 and modulo x − 3. It also preserves all the ring operations. Furthermore, if a polynomial is divisible by both x − 2 and x − 3 , then it’s divisible by their product. Therefore, it’s injective, so it’s an isomorphism. Furthermore Z [ x ] / ( x − 2 ) is isomorphic to Z by evaluating a polynomial at x = 2. Also, Z [ x ] / ( x − 3 ) is isomorphic to Z . Composing the isomorphisms, Z [ x ] / ( ( x − 2 ) ( x − 3 ) ) is isomorphic to Z × Z . This composition takes a polynomial and evaluates it at x = 2 and at x = 3. This should remind you of the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

Question: How can anyone take math and physics seriously enough to devote a career to them, (overwhelming evidence that the material universe obeys mathematics) without positing that abstract entities have an independent existence outside the human mind?

Question: Can any real number be represented as an infinite product of prime powers, allowing negative exponents?
Answer: I’ll assume you’re only allowing integer powers. If you have an infinite product of numbers that converges to any number other than 0, the terms in that product have to approach 1. If they don’t approach 1, the product doesn't converge to a nonzero number. What prime power is close to 1? If p is a prime number, then p to a positive power is at least p , and that’s not close to 1. But p to a negative power is less than or equal to 1 / p , and that’s also not close to 1. In order the the terms to approach 1, they all have to eventually equal 1. That means the infinite product is really just a finite product. Zero can be expressed as the product of the reciprocals of all the prime numbers. Every positive rational number can be expressed as a finite product of primes to integer powers, but no other number can be.

Question: Does defining the real numbers via Dedekind cuts imply the least upper bound property of the reals, or does it require you to assume in advance that the real numbers have the l. u. b. property? Or neither?
Answer: Definition of the real numbers The real numbers can be abstractly defined as a complete ordered field. A complete ordered field is an ordered field that has the least upper bound property. Definitions don’t show things exist. Defining real numbers as a complete ordered field doesn’t show that there is anything that actually is a complete ordered field, that is, a model for the definition. Some construction is needed to show there exists a complete ordered field. One thing that you can show from the definition is that there is that for any two complete ordered fields there is a unique isomorphism between them. Essentially, that means that the only difference between them are the names you use for their elements. Construction by Dedekind cuts You can construct a model for the real numbers by means of Dedekind cuts on the rational numbers. You then have to prove that the resulting set is a complete ordered field. One part of that is proving that what you’ve constructed has the least upper bound property. Other constructions There are other constructions of the real numbers that don’t used Dedekind cuts. For any one of those, in order to know that construction results in the real numbers, you have to prove that construction gives a complete ordered field. One other construction uses Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Another uses decimal representations. Once constructed, you can discard the construction The purpose of that construction is to show that the real numbers exists. Once you’ve done that, you don’t need to refer to the details of the construction again. That’s because there can be only one model of real numbers up to unique isomorphism.

Question: Can we turn every group into a vector space?
Answer: No, you can’t if you want the vector space to have the same elements as the group. For example, there is a group with six elements, but no vector space over any scalar field whatsoever has six elements. There are, however, ways of representing groups in terms of vector spaces and linear algebra. One way is to take a vector space with a basis with the same number of elements as the group, then each element of the group determines a linear transformation (a matrix) on that vector space. Here’s an example of that. Let the group be the cyclic group with three elements. G = { e , a , a 2 } where e is the identity element of the group, and a 3 = e . Then the vector space R G has dimension 3. Each element of R G is a linear combination ( x , y , z ) = x e + y a + z a 2 of the three basis elements e , a , and a 2 . The group G can be represented as a subgroup of the general linear group, i.e., the group of nonsingular linear transformations (3 by 3 matrices) on the vector space. e corresponds to the identity matrix. a corresponds to the matrix ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 0 1 0 0 0 1 1 0 0 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ and a 2 to the square of that matrix. The subject of representing groups this way is called representation theory. See for more on it.

Question: What is an isomorphism?
Answer: In mathematics, the term isomorphism is used for a lot of things all of which are special cases of isomorphisms in category theory. Definition of category A category in mathematics has objects and morphisms between objects. Typically objects are denoted with capital letters like A and B , while morphisms are denoted with lower case letters like f and g . Each morphism f has a domain object A and a codomain object B . That’s denoted f : A → B . When the codomain of one morphism is the same as the domain of another, then they can be composed to give a third morphism. More precisely, if f : A → B and g : B → C , then their composition is a morphism g ∘ f : A → C . Also, each object A has an associated identity morphism 1 A : A → A . Given a morphism f : A → B , the compositions f ∘ 1 A and 1 B ∘ f both are equal to f itself. Finally, composition is associative: h ∘ ( g ∘ f ) = ( h ∘ g ) ∘ f when f : A → B , g : B → C , and h : C → D . Examples of categories One example is the category of groups. The objects are groups and the morphisms are group homomorphisms. Another example is the category of rings. The objects are rings and the morphisms are ring homomorphisms. Another is the category of sets. Objects are sets, and morphisms are functions. Another is the category of topological spaces. Objects are topological spaces, and morphisms are continuous functions. Isomorphisms in a category An isomorphism is a morphism f : A → B such that there exists another morphism g : B → A such that both g ∘ f = 1 A and f ∘ G = 1 B . When f is an isomorphism, you can show that there is only one such g , so that g can be denoted f − 1 . Furthermore, f − 1 is an isomorphism f − 1 : B → A . Isomorphisms are important in that any categorical thing you can say about an object you can also say about objects that are isomorphic to it. Essentially, the only thing different about isomorphic objects are their names. Examples of isomorphisms In the category of groups, an isomorphism is called a group isomorphism. In the category of rings, an isomorphism is called a ring isomorphism. In the category of sets, an isomorphism is called a bijection. In the category of topological spaces, an isomorphism is called a homeomorphism. Isomorphisms in different categories are different Different names for isomorphisms are used in different categories. Sometimes something can be thought of as being an object in more than one category. For example, a topological group is a group if you forget its topology, but it’s a topological space if you forget its group structure, and it’s a set if you forget both. You could have a function between two of them that’s an isomorphism in one category, but not in another. It could be a discontinuous group isomorphism, or a homeomorphism that is not a group isomorphism, or just a bijection that’s neither continuous nor preserves the group structure.

Question: Why are alphabets in mathematics?
Answer: The term “alphabet” is used in the theory of formal languages. Formal languages talk about “strings” which are finite lists of “letters”, the “letters” are elements of a set called the “alphabet”. Here’s an example. Let the alphabet consist of two symbols, a , and b . The alphabet under discussion is usually denoted with a capital sigma, so Σ = { a , b } . If you have a list consisting of a repeated three times, that’s called a string or word, and it’s denoted a a a . The word consisting of a followed by b and then another a and b is denoted a b a b . The set of all possible words is denoted Σ ∗ . The asterisk is used in this theory to denoted any number of repetitions, including no repetitions. That means there’s a word of length zero. Depending on the textbook, the empty word is denoted λ or ϵ . The notation a ∗ denotes the set of all words consisting of the letter a repeated any number of times. So a ∗ = { λ , a , a a , a a a , a a a a , … } . For more on formal languages, see answers to the question What is the point of formal language? and What is formal language theory?

Question: I read somewhere that polynomials can be formally defined by sequences, but I haven't found anything relevant on the web. So, my question is, are polynomials defined by sequences, and if yes how?
Answer: You can do that for polynomials of one variable when the variable is suppressed. That way a polynomial like 4 − 2 x 2 − 5 x 3 is the same thing as 4 − 2 t 2 − 5 t 3 . One way to do that to treat the polynomial as a sequence of coefficients where the sequence has only finitely many nonzero terms. So the polynomial mentioned above is treated as the sequence ( 4 , 0 , − 2 , − 5 , 0 , … ) where all the terms after − 5 are zero. With that definition, addition and subtraction are done coordinatewise. Multiplication, of course, is more complicated. ( a 0 , a 1 , a 2 , … ) ( b 0 , b 1 , b 2 , … ) = ( a 0 b 0 , a 0 b 1 + a 1 b 0 , a 0 b 2 + a 1 b 1 + a 2 b 0 , … ) where the n t h term of the product is ∑ n k = 0 a k b n − k . Without the condition that the sequence has only finitely many nonzero terms, you can define formal power series in the same way. The advantage of making a definition like this is that polynomials can be easily defined in terms of set theory. You don’t have to decide what a variable is supposed to be.

Question: Suppose that A and B are two propositions. What is the logic formula for which A does not imply B? Is it \neg (A\implies B) or A\implies\neg B?
Answer: To say “A does not imply B” says “it is not the case that A does imply B”. That’s ¬ ( A → B ) . It’s only false when P is true and Q is false. So ¬ ( A → B ) is logically equivalent to A ∧ ¬ B , while A → ¬ B is logically equivalent to ¬ A ∨ ¬ B . They’re quite different.

Question: How do I prove that this is tautology without using prove table: (p → q) → ((r ∨ p) → (r∨ q))?

Question: Why does 1/3 give 0.333, but 1/7 doesn't give a similar pattern?
Answer: All rational numbers eventually have a repeating pattern. The only ones that have a repeating pattern of length 1 are those whose denominators divide 9. So, for example, 1 3 is 0.333 … where the 3 repeats forever. The part that repeats is usually shown with a bar over it as in 1 3 = 0. ¯¯¯ 3 . Likewise, 4 9 = 0. ¯¯¯ 4 . The only rational numbers whose repetition length can be 2 or less are those whose denominators divide 99. Since 99 has a factor of 11, then fractions with denominators of 11 have repetition length 2. For example, 4 11 = 0. ¯¯¯¯¯¯ 36 . To get a repetition length of 3, the denominator has to divide 999. The prime factorization of 999 is 3 3 ⋅ 37. So 3 37 = 0. ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ 081 repeats every three digits. Since 7 doesn’t divide 9, or 99, or 999, or 9999, or 99999, 1 7 can’t have a repetition length of 5 or less. But 7 does divide 999999, and 1 7 = 0. ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ 142857 , and 4 7 = 0. ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ 571428 . Both have repetition length of 6. In general, the repetition length of a fraction with denominator n is always less than n . Furthermore, that length will divide ϕ ( n ) , the number of positive integers less than n relatively prime to n .

Question: Did the ancient Egyptians and Greeks know about the golden ratio and how did they utilize it in the Parthenon and pyramids?
Answer: There’s no reason to believe that the ancient Egyptians knew about it. It’s possible they did, but there is no evidence that they did. Claims that it appears somehow in the pyramids are as bogus as claims that π appears somehow in the pyramids. Greek geometers knew of the ratio that we call the golden ratio. It is the ratio of a diagonal of a regular pentagon to the side of that pentagon. Euclid and his predecessors Eudoxus and Theaetetus knew and used it in geometry. There’s no reason to think that it was used in the Parthenon or any other ancient buildings. It didn’t become popular outside of mathematics until Paccioli (1447–1517) wrote about it and called it the “divine proportion”. He found it fascinating, even mystical, but before that it was only one of many geometric ratios.

Question: Is there any order relation on the ring of formal power series with real coefficients which makes this ring an ordered ring?
Answer: Yes, treat the variable as a positive infinitesimal. (You can do the same thing with polynomials, of course.) A power series a 0 + a 1 x + a 2 x 2 + a 3 x 3 + ⋯ with real coefficients is positive when its first nonzero coefficient is positive; negative when its first nonzero coefficient is negative; and only the power series with all zero coefficients is zero. For example, 3 − 5 x + 8 x 2 + ⋯ is positive since 3 is positive, but − 5 x + 8 x 2 + ⋯ is negative since –5 is negative, and 8 x 2 + ⋯ is positive since 8 is positive. That last one is an infinitesimal since it’s positive but less than every positive real number.

Question: If a real vector space is just a set of tuples, why why the elements (0, 1) and (1, 0) are visualized as perpendicular? A tuple is just the list of numbers and there is no concept of angle for lists.
Answer: Vector spaces A real vector space isn’t just a set of tuples. There are other things than just elements that are required for a vector space. Furthermore, angles require more than just a vector space. A vector space doesn’t just have elements (which are called vectors), those vectors can be added. That addition is required to satisfy the usual properties of addition and subtraction. Besides addition, a real vector space is required to have a way of multiplying vectors by real numbers (called scalar multiplication). Scalar multiplication is required to satisfy the usual properties of multiplication such as distributivity of multiplication over addition. Inner product spaces Real vector spaces by themselves don’t have enough structure to define angles. More is needed for angles. That’s a dot product (also called inner product). Given two vectors v and w , they determine a scalar, called their dot product, which is denoted v ⋅ w . It has to satisfy certain properties, too, such as distributivity over addition. Once a dot product is specified, length of vectors (also called their norm) can be defined by ∥ v ∥ = √ v ⋅ v , and the angle θ between two vectors v and w can be defined by θ = arccos v ⋅ w ∥ v ∥ ∥ w ∥ . In particular, two vectors are at right angles when v ⋅ w = 0. The standard structure on R × R Ordered pairs of real numbers have a standard vector space structure and an inner product space structure. Addition is defined by adding coordinatewise. ( v 1 , v 2 ) + ( w 1 , w 2 ) is defined to be ( v 1 + w 1 , v 2 + w 2 ) . Scalar multiplication for a real number a is defined so that a ( v 1 , v 2 ) is equal to ( a v 1 , a v 2 ) . With those definitions, R 2 is a vector space. The dot product is defined by ( v 1 , v 2 ) ⋅ ( w 1 , w 2 ) = v 1 w 1 + v 2 w 2 . Two vectors are at right angles when v 1 w 1 + v 2 w 2 = 0. In particular, ( 0 , 1 ) and ( 1 , 0 ) are perpendicular. With this standard structure, ordered pairs in R 2 can be identified as usual in the standard way as points in a plane. That’s sometimes called the Cartesian plane (after Descartes) and sometimes called the Euclidean plane.

Question: According to many sources, non-square matrices have no determinant since volume is squished, making the volume 0, but how do you find the remaining area determinant that results from that squish? Sure, it doesn't have any volume, but it has area.
Answer: If you want the following two properties about determinants to hold, then there’s no possible value for the determinant of a non-square matrix. Suppose that the determinant of a non-square matrix A is d . Then the determinant of its transpose A T is also d . Therefore, both A T A and A A T have the same determinant d 2 . Take this example. A = ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 1 0 0 1 0 0 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ so that A T = [ 1 0 0 0 1 0 ] Then A T A is the 2 × 2 identity matrix with determinant 1. But A A T = ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ has determinant 0. Since 1 does not equal 0, there’s no possible value for the determinant of A . (It doesn’t depend on volume or area or any geometric concept, just those two properties.) So determinants are only defined for square matrices.

Question: Why do people not homeschool their children when it is well known that kids whose parents are very involved in their education, do better in school?
Answer: You say in your question that “kids whose parents are very involved in their education, do better in school.” That’s probably true. Then you ask “why don’t people homeschool their children?” Teaching is difficult. If you want your children to learn, a teacher can do it well. Most parents can’t. Teaching takes time. Parents often don’t have the time to teach their children. There are other considerations that aren’t so closely tied to education like socialization with other children. Question: If the Type O allele is recessive and the other blood types A, B and AB are all dominant, wouldn't type O's have been completely bred out by now after thousands of years of procreating? Same for Rh factors?
Answer: That’s not how dominant and recessive work. “Dominant” as used in genetics doesn’t mean domination over time. It just means that only one copy of the gene is necessary to be expressed. Recessive means that two copies are needed. Say there are two alleles, one dominant denoted D and the other recessive denoted d. An individual could be DD (two copies of D), or Dd (one of each), or dd (two copies of d). Those that are DD and Dd will express the dominant trait; those that are dd will express the recessive trait. Unless one of those two traits is more fit, the proportions of DD, Dd, and dd in the population is stable. The proportions won’t change in a large population at all. In a smaller population it could drift to favor more D’s or more d’s, but neither is more likely. If it happens that one of the two traits endows the holder with more “fitness” than the other, then that trait will be selected for, and the other selected against, so over time the less fit allele will be bred out. I don’t happen to know if any of these blood types are more “fit” than others. It can be complicated since one type could be better in some ways, but another type in other ways.

Question: If group theory is related to symmetry, how about the other topics of abstract algebra, which are rings, fields, modules, and ideals? How can I understand them with specific examples?

Some are like the field Q of rational numbers, R of real numbers, and C of complex numbers. But there are others like the finite fields and function fields. Rings include fields but are more general. The elements can be added, subtracted, and multiplied, but division isn’t required. The ring of integers Z is a ring, as is R [ x ] , the ring of polynomials with real coefficients. There are lots of other rings. Modules and ideals use rings in their definitions, and they’re used to study number theory and algebraic geometry. Algebraic geometry studies algebraic curves and other algebraic varieties that are defined in terms of algebraic equations. Cubic curves are examples of those. Groups are specifically the abstraction of symmetries. There are other algebraic structures for other purposes. Question: How can we give an example of a non-abelian group such that every subgroup of G is normal in G?

In fact, the smallest Hamiltonian group is the quaternion group Q 8 which has eight elements. Dedekind studied these groups at the end of the 19th century. Of course, every subgroup of an Abelian group is normal, but he wondered what other subgroups have this property. He proved that all of them involve Q 8 somehow. In particular each Hamiltonian group is the direct product of Q 8 and an Abelian group A . Not every Abelian group A works to make Q 8 × A a Hamiltonian group, and Dedekind characterized which ones do.

As I read more, I get pieces and ideas of where this new mathematics fits in. When I have time, I’ll look at the historical context. I read what other people say about where it comes from. This secondhand information is necessarily simplified since the real history is much more complicated. You may recall hearing, for example, that calculus was discovered independently by Newton and Leibniz. Yet almost all of calculus was developed either before them or after them. There are books on the history of calculus, and they can’t even cover it all. You might expect that if you just read the original works of mathematics, that would do it. But no, that leads to more questions since nothing is created without a context. Also, the original mathematics is much harder to understand than modern expositions of it. So do try to figure out how things you’re studying came to be, that is, their historical context, but don’t expect to find a complete answer, and do expect it to be much more complicated than just studying the things themselves.

That means you need to prove that the given property holds for all the sets of cardinality κ 0 . Next prove the inductive step that P n implies P n + 1 . Question: How can Platonism be avoided with the fact that the Pythagorean theorem is true, but not because Pythagoras said so, it is also always true and It was true before Pythagoras, and it is still true after?
Answer: Mathematics is entirely independent of your personal opinion concerning Platonism. You can avoid it since it has no effect on what is or is not a theorem. A theorem is a statement for which there is a proof that follows from the axioms. Take, for example, the statement that the square of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of its two legs. That’s a theorem in Euclidean geometry because there is a proof that follows from the axioms of Euclidean geometry. (Pythagoras may or may not have had a proof of it, but Euclid certainly did.) There’s a connection between proofs and truth, but they’re different things. Whether a statement is true depends on what you’re talking about. Take again the statement that the square of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of its two legs.It’s not true on the surface of the Earth, even if you idealize that surface as a perfect sphere. It is true for the coordinate geometry of R 2 with the usual meanings of distance and angle. The connection between proofs and truth is that if you’ve got something for which the axioms of a theory are all true, then the theorems of that theory will also be all true. In R 2 all the axioms of Euclidean geometry are true, so all the theorems, including the Pythagorean theorem, are also true. But the axioms of Euclidean geometry aren’t all true for a sphere, and the Pythagorean theorem isn’t true either.

Question: How come a grand conspiracy exists among trig teachers to hide the regular pentagon and the values of circular functions at the pentagonal angles from their students?
Answer: I think your question is why the sine, cosine, and tangent of 72° and related angles of 18°, 36°, and 54° aren’t mentioned in trigonometry textbooks and courses. There are certain specific acute angles whose trig functions are mentioned including 45°, 30°, and 60°. Those particular angles come up more often than others since the 30°-60°-90° triangle and the 45°-45°-90° triangle occur often as squares and equilateral triangles are common. The 18°-72°-90° triangle and the 36°-54°-90° arise from regular pentagons, and they don’t appear as often. Applications come from all sorts of places besides abstract geometry, and for those other applications, all angles are relevant, not just those common ones. Ptolemy created a table of trig functions to deal with them about 1900 years ago, and tables, slide rules, computers, and calculators deal with arbitrary angles. There’s no grand conspiracy. It’s just that the angles from pentagons aren’t especially important. Because of that, the trig functions of those angles are not mentioned in textbooks and courses. I imagine a lot of high school teachers don’t even know about them. But I think they should be mentioned. Not because of their applications, but because of their history and the importance of them in the development of mathematics and trigonometry. Ptolemy could create his tables because he knew about those angles. They had been studied by the Pythagoreans, and they’re prominent in Euclid’s Elements. Although the concept of degrees for measuring angles postdates Euclid, nonetheless, those angles appear. They are important in the analysis and construction of regular pentagons, regular dodecahedra, and regular icosahedra. If you don’t know about this yourself, you can discover it all starting with the 36°-72°-72° isosceles triangle. The only thing you need to know about it is that the ratio of a long side to the short side is 1 2 ( 1 + √ 5 ) . That’s what Euclid called extreme and mean ratio, but now known as the golden ratio. Question: Is it true that although π can be approx. with some infinite series, there is no known infinite series for π that is π directly? Is it true that no matter the known infinite series we use to approximate π, it won't be accurate after a lot of places?
Answer: There are many infinite series whose sums are exactly π . If you don’t sum all the terms, however, you won’t get the sum of the entire series. That means that the partial sums are only approximations. The sum of the entire series, however, is precisely π . Take this infinite series π 2 + π 4 + π 8 + ⋯ where each term is half the preceding one. The sum of the infinite series is precisely π . It’s not surprising that if you don’t add all the terms, you won’t get π . If you only add the first 3 terms, that partial sum is only 7 8 π . Of course, that series isn’t helpful if you want to figure out what π is since you need to know π in order to evaluate each of the terms. Here’s just one of many series that can be used to find π π 2 = 1 + 1 3 + 1 ⋅ 2 3 ⋅ 5 + 1 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 3 3 ⋅ 5 ⋅ 7 + ⋯ It converges just a little faster than the first series since each term is less than half of the previous term.

Question: Is it possible that the ZFC axioms are inconsistent, but nonetheless true? I'm having a hard time understanding how Con(ZFC) could be independent of the axioms.
Answer: In order to call a statement in a theory true, there needs to be a model for the theory in which every statement is either true or its negation is true (but not both), and all the axioms of the theory are true. In that case the statement is true in that model. It may be false in other models, so truth is relative to a particular model. If a theory has a model, then it’s a consistent theory. That’s because in the model, the axioms of the theory are true, and the only theorems that can be proved in the theory are true in every model. If a theory is inconsistent, it has no model. So the answer to the question is NO. If there’s anyway to interpret the axioms as true, then the theory is consistent. As far as understanding how a statement could be independent, keep in mind that in an incomplete theory there are a lot of independent statements. ZFC, if consistent, is incomplete. (That follows from Gödel’s incompleteness theorem for number theory, and number theory can be expressed in set theory.) A statement like Con(ZFC) could be one of those independent statements.

Question: What color can most animals not see?
Answer: Do you mean what spectrum colors can’t most animals see? Humans, for example, see a range of spectrum colors from red through violet. We can’t see infrared beyond red, and we can’t see ultraviolet beyond violet. Many animals have about the same range, but birds and insects can see into the ultraviolet range, and various animals can see into the infrared. On the whole, however, our range is typical. There’s more to colors than spectrum colors. What colors an animal can distinguish depends on what kinds of color receptors they have in their eyes. With our night vision, we can barely distinguish colors at all since night vision depends on rods, and there’s only one kind of rod, while day vision depends on cones, and there are three kinds of cones. During the day, we can distinguish lots of different colors, but at night only shades of gray. Many mammals (and colorblind people) only have two kinds of cones, so they can’t distinguish as many colors. They can still see colors of the spectrum from red to violet, but some of them look similar. Other animals have more than three kinds of cones, so they can distinguish more colors than animals that have only three kinds. (And it gets more complicated than just spectrum colors since mixtures of colors can also be distinguished like magenta, brown, and pink, not to mention white and gray.) A reasonable answer would be that most animals can’t see ultraviolet or infrared.

Question: What do the letters mean in algebra? Why don't they just use numbers?
Answer: Letters (that is, variables) are pronouns like “it”, “she”, and “he”. They refer to something, typically an unknown number. You can use them in sentences, usually sentences that say one thing is equal to another. Such sentences can be abbreviated using symbols. For example, if you know 3 times some number is equal to 36 more than it, you can write that as 3 x = 36 + x where x is the pronoun which refers to that number. Question: A imaginary number is composed of real number and imaginary number. But those have different units..how can you represent something with two units?
Answer: Perhaps you’re taking “imaginary number” to be a purely imaginary number. That’s a complex number whose real part is zero. Question: How do you find quantifiers?
Answer: I think you’re asking how to identify quantifiers in English sentences. In general it’s not easy to identify quantifiers. There are a lot of words that can indicate quantifiers. Some of them are easy to see like “all”, “each”, and “every”. Those indicate universal quantifiers. In the sentence “Every dog has its day” the word “dog” is universally quantified. It means the same thing as “Each dog has its day,” and “All dogs have their day.” Sometimes the universal quantifier doesn’t appear as in “Dogs have their day.” Existential quantifiers are sometimes explicit. In the sentences “There is a dog that has its day,” and “At least one dog has its day,” the word “dog” is existentially quantified as it is in “Some dog has its day.” Sometimes existential quantifiers include the numerical information as well as in “Exactly one dog has its day,” or “There are hundreds of dogs that have their day.” Note that the word “the” in “The dog has its day” refers to a specific dog that is under consideration. There has to be an antecedent for that sentence to have a meaning, just like “it” in “It has its day” requires an antecedent. The word “any” sometimes indicates a universal quantifier but sometimes indicates an existential quantifier. In “Any dog has its day,” it’s a universal quantifier, but in the question “Do you know of any dog that has its day?” it’s an existential quantifier. The words “a” and “an” usually indicate existential quantifiers, but sometimes universal quantifiers. Does “A dog has its day” have a universal quantifier or an existential quantifier. The context might make a difference Quantifiers can hide in other words as well. Take “Every sufficiently old dog will have its day” for example. Certainly “every” indicates a universal quantifier, but the adverb “sufficiently” indicates an existential quantifier. A wordier version of that sentence is “There is an age such that for each dog of at least that age, that dog will have its day.” That’s an example of nested quantifiers. The outer quantifier is “there is” while the inner quantifier is “for each”. The order of nested quantifiers can make a difference. “Every person has some woman as a mother” doesn’t mean the same thing as “Some woman is the mother of every person” even though both sentences have a universal and an existential quantifier.

Question: How can you show that any set containing the single non-zero vector is linearly independent?
Answer: The general definition of linear dependence and linear independence A set of vectors is linearly dependent when there is a nonzero linear combination that sums to the zero vector. In symbols, that says the set { v 1 , v 2 , … , v k } is a linearly dependent set when there are scalars c 1 , c 2 , … , c k , not all zero, such that c 1 v 1 + c 2 v 2 + ⋯ + c k v k = 0 . Otherwise, they’re linearly independent. An equivalent condition is that one of the vectors is a linear combination of the rest. The case of two vectors Before going on the the case of one vector, let’s look at the case of two vectors. Two vectors v and w are linearly dependent when there exist two scalars c and d , not both zero, such that c v + d w = 0 . That’s equivalent to saying that at least one of them is a scalar multiple of the other. When c ≠ 0 , that implies v = − ( d / c ) w making v a scalar multiple of w . Likewise, if d ≠ 0 then w a scalar multiple of v . When neither is a scalar multiple of the other, the two vectors are linearly independent. The case of one vector What does it mean to say that a set consisting of only one vector is linearly dependent? To say the singleton set consisting of the vector v is linearly dependent means that there is a nonzero scalar c such that c v = 0 . Since c ≠ 0 , that means v = 0 . Therefore, a single vector is linearly dependent only when that vector is the zero vector. The set v consisting of a single vector is independent if and only if that vector is not the zero vector.

Question: How can you prove in quantifiers and mathematical logic that the intersection of sets of equivalent relations is equivalent, while their union is not necessarily?
Answer: The intersection of two equivalence relations is another equivalence relation. The same can’t be said for unions. (Recall that an equivalence relation on a set is a binary relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.) Intersections of equivalence relations Let ∼ and ≅ be two equivalence relations on a set. Define their intersection ≡ by saying x ≡ y when both x ∼ y and x ≅ y . You can easily show ≡ is also reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Here’s the proof of transitivity. Given that x ≡ y and y ≡ z , to show x ≡ z . Since x ≡ y , therefore both x ∼ y and x ≅ y . Also, since y ≡ z , therefore both y ∼ z and y ≅ z . Since both ∼ and ≅ are transitive, therefore both x ∼ z and x ≅ z . Thus, x ≡ z . (The only way that quantifiers are used in this proof is that x , y , and z are all universally quantified.) The proofs that ≡ is reflexive and symmetric are shorter. Unions of equivalence relations It isn’t true that the union of two equivalence relations is always an equivalence relation. In fact, that rarely happens. You construct a counterexample, take a set with three elements { a , b , c } Let a ∼ b and b ≅ c , but neither relate a to c . Then their union will relate a to b and b to c , but not a to c .

Question: Some authors of Linear Algebra use vectors as row matrices, while others use them as column matrices. Why?
Answer: For reasons of history, typesetting, and writing vectors so they don’t take too much space in books, n-vectors are often written as n-tuples. For example, a vector in 3-space might be written ( 5 , 2 , 6 ) . Now consider a linear transformation which sends ( x , y , z ) to ( 2 x + y , 2 y + z , 2 z + x ) . It sends ( 5 , 2 , 6 ) to ( 12 , 10 , 17 ) . Vectors as column matrices Most textbooks will encode the linear transformation as the matrix and treat the vector as a column matrix ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 2 1 0 0 2 1 1 0 2 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 5 2 6 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ = ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 12 10 17 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ . The problem with that it’s written horizontally as a 3-tuple, but needs to be converted to a vertical column matrix. Vectors as row matrices If you leave the vector as a row matrix, you’ll need to put it on the left because of the way matrix multiplication is defined. But that means you’ll need a different matrix for the linear transformation (the transpose of the one above). [ 5 2 6 ] ⎡ ⎢ ⎣ 2 0 1 1 2 0 0 1 2 ⎤ ⎥ ⎦ = [ 12 10 17 ] History In the 1850s Cayley developed the theory of matrices. Since transformations are functions, and in functional notation the function is written to the left of the argument, he placed vectors to the right of the matrix as column vectors. Furthermore, he defined multiplication of vectors to correspond to evaluation of linear transformations, and more generally to composition of linear transformations. Some authors in the 1900s made vectors of row matrices, perhaps so that n-tuples could be treated as row matrices. Most follow Cayley and use column matrices for vectors. Question: Does Rolle's theorem only guarantee that there is a point where f'(c) =0 or does it guarantee a local maximum/minimum in the interval? If only that f'(c) =0 does this mean that the guaranteed point could be an inflection point an not a local max/min?
Answer: The usual statement of Rolle’s theorem just says that there is somewhere where the derivative is zero, but the standard proof also shows that is either a local maximum or local minimum. Here’s the statement of Rolle’s theorem. Rolle’s theorem. If a function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior, and it takes the same value at both endpoints of the interval, then somewhere on the open interval the function has a zero derivative. Below is an outline of a standard proof. That depends on the extremal value theorem (EVT) and a previously proved theorem. The EVT says that functions that are continuous on a closed interval take on both a minimum and a maximum value. The previously proved theorem says that says if a function takes on an extreme value (either a max or a min) at a point in an open interval where it’s differentiable, then the derivative of the function is zero there. Proof of Rolle’s theorem. Since the function is continuous on a closed interval, by the EVT it has both a maximum and a minimum value. The previously proved theorem says that if either of them occur at an interior point, then the derivative is zero there which proves Rolle’s theorem. But if both extrema occur at the endpoints, then, since the function has the same value at both endpoints, the function is constant, so the derivative is zero at every interior point. So you see from the proof that the place where the derivative is shown to be zero has either the maximum or minimum value on the interval (or both if the function is constant).
