Question: With cantor’s set theory, which is non-axiomatic - what does it MEAN (besides not having axioms) to be non-axiomatic? What are the axioms replaced with to make the system logically valid yet still be “non-axiomatic”?
Answer: Logic itself wasn’t formalized in the late 1800s, but it was pretty well understood. The idea of sets (called various different things in different languages, and in English “systems” was more common) was pretty well understood. A set was supposed to collect things together so you could talk about them. If you had a concept, like the concept of odd number, then there was a set of all the the things that satisfied that concept, the set of odd numbers. It seems like a pretty innocuous idea. Various logical connectives correspond to operations on sets. Conjunction — AND — corresponds to intersection. If you have two sets, then their intersection consists of those things that belong to both. The union of two sets consists of those things that belong to at least one of the two sets. The complement of one set in another consists of all the things in the other set that aren't in the first set. These operations were used by Boole, De Morgan, and others much earlier in the 1800s. The empty set wasn’t universally accepted. Dedekind, one of the founders of set theory, rejected empty sets. He only accepted intersections of two sets if they weren’t disjoint. Cantor had good reasons to include the empty set, and so do we. It’s not just set theory that didn’t have axioms, number theory didn't either. In the 1860s Hermann Grassmann wrote a book proving all the basic properties of integers, but he didn’t use any axioms. In fact, he rejected the axiomatic method. He did describe the principle of mathematical induction and used it in his proofs, but he didn’t take it as an axiom. In 1888 Dedekind did something similar for positive integers basing his proofs on informal set theory. He, too missed an important axiom, the one that says there’s an infinite set. His proofs are all good except his proof that there’s an infinite set. That depends on making his thoughts into sets. So that’s the first serious problem with set theory, the existence of an infinite set. It should be an axiom. Cantor went further and built sets whose elements were sets themselves. In particular, he used power sets of sets. The elements of a power set of sets are the subsets of that set. So that’s the second serious problem that should have been addressed by positing an axiom. As you probably know, in the early 1900s Russell found a contradiction in informal set theory, and soon after Zermelo developed a theory of set theory based on axioms that aren’t strong enough to imply Russell’s contradiction. So, what was set theory before it had axioms? It was informal, like number theory was, and like algebra was, and like calculus was, and what logic itself was. As long as people understood what principles were allowed in proofs, and as long as those principles didn’t lead to contradictions, that seemed to be enough.

Question: If the solar system really exists, how do solar systems explain that the sun is a hyperhot ball of fire even though there is no oxygen in space and fire needs oxygen for combustion?
Answer: This question couldn’t have been asked until (1) oxygen was discovered, (2) it was determined that fire needs oxygen to burn, and (3) it was determined that there is no oxygen in space. Joseph Priestly and others determined (1) and (2) in the 1770s. They were trying to determine how burning works. After burning something in an enclosed jar, it used up something in the air. That something could be slowly replenished by a plant growing in the jar. Lavoisier called that something “oxygen”. Back then the sun could still be explained as a big fire consuming massive amounts of fire. By the mid 1800s, though, it was determined that a big burning ball like that couldn’t last more than a few thousand years because it would exhaust the fuel it was burning. Chemical reactions couldn’t sustain the sun. So the question returned: how is the sun producing so much energy? Several hypotheses were proposed to answer that question like gravitational collapse and meteors falling into the sun. None were particularly convincing. Also in the 1800s the spectrum of light coming from the sun was the same as ionized plasma, so whatever the explanation was, it had to involve ionized plasma. Hydrogen, helium, and other elements were discovered that century, and from further spectroscopic analysis of sunlight, it was determined that the sun was mostly hydrogen and helium, and very little oxygen. For decades there was no good explanation of how the sun worked. Finally, in the early 1900s, the new field of nuclear physics gave the answer: fusion. It’s not a chemical reaction at all, but a nuclear reaction. Hydrogen fuses together to create helium, and in the process a lot of energy is created. No oxygen is needed.

Question: If infinite never ends, why can one infinite number be larger than another?
Answer: The ordinary numbers don’t include any infinite numbers, so you must be talking about something else. There are several concepts in mathematics that include things called infinite numbers. You may be thinking of one of those things. Leibniz used infinitesimals which are less than all the usual positive numbers, and their reciprocals are infinite. Cantor had both infinite ordinal numbers and infinite cardinal numbers. Conway’s surreal numbers include infinite numbers, too. It’s just that never ending doesn’t come into it. Take this sequence of numbers: 1 − 1 2 , 1 − 1 4 , 1 − 1 8 , 1 − 1 16 , ⋯ where each number in the sequence halves the distance left to the number 1. It never ends, but there are lots of numbers greater than any of them, for example, 1 and 2. Just because you can keep listing things forever doesn’t mean you’ve listed them all. For each of the concepts in the second paragraph of this answer, there’s something analogous where after every infinite number there are lots more after it.

Question: Based on Godel's incompleteness theorem, is it correct to conclude that the formal system either includes an undecidable proposition or is an inconsistent system?
Answer: It depends on the formal system you’re talking about. Euclidean geometry is a formal system that is consistent and complete. It has no undecidable propositions. For each statement either it or its negation is provable from the axioms but not both. Peano arithmetic is not complete. As Gödel showed, there are statements for which neither the statement nor its negation can be proved from the axioms. Furthermore, any consistent theory that contains Peano arithmetic for which there’s an algorithm to list all the axioms is also not complete. It’s important to include the requirement that the axioms be listable, for if not, you could just take all true statements about numbers to be the axioms. That’s a consistent and complete theory.

Question: What is the mathematical significance of Gödel's incompleteness theorems, and how do they impact our understanding of formal systems?
Answer: Formal logic and axioms for number theory and set theory were developed in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The hope and expectation was that anything that was true about numbers could be proved from the Dedekind-Peano axioms. If so, then mathematics could even be carried out by an algorithm. Gödel’s incompleteness theorem showed otherwise. The Dedekind-Peano axioms aren’t complete. There are statements about number theory that don’t follow from those axioms, and their negations also don’t follow from the axioms. Furthermore, any first-order extension of the Dedekind-Peano axioms that’s effective and consistent won’t be complete. (Effective means the axioms can be listed, and consistent means it can’t prove 0=1.) What does that mean? It doesn’t effect anything that can be proved. All of mathematics remains intact. It does mean mathematics is more complicated than was thought back in 1900. There is no algorithm to decide whether a statement in number theory can be proved or not.

Question: What is concept of functions according to father of math?
Answer: There is no “father of math”. Mathematics developed over thousands of years, and many people, both men and women, contributed. The concept of function isn’t that old, however. It’s four or five hundred years old, and the concept has changed over the centuries. Formulas In the 1600s and 1700s as symbolic algebra, coordinate geometry, and mathematical analysis developed, a function meant a formula with an independent variable and another variable dependent on it. Something like y = x 2 + sin 2 x described a function. Sometimes the formula wasn’t known, so the problem was to find a formula. The problem might be described by a differential equation, and the solution might involve integration. It was all very intuitive. Newton, for example, assumed that every function was differentiable, although that wasn’t stated explicitly. Functional notation began to be used in the 1700s. The notation f ( x ) = x 2 + sin x not only describes a function, but it gives a name f for that function. Having names for things aids in thinking of them as things in themselves. Abstract functions Fourier series expanded the concept of function. They seemed to be formulas, but they described functions that needn’t be differentiable or even continuous. The question was, what exactly is a function? In the 1800s it was clarified that all that was necessary for a function was to give a specific output (dependent variable) for each given input (independent variable). The concept of domain was developed, the domain being for which values of the independent variable there is any output at all. For example, y = 1 / x excludes 0 from the domain since 1 / 0 doesn’t have a value. Notice that this concept of function is not the same as a formula or a rule. Different formulas or rules can describe the same function. For example, both x 2 − 4 and ( x + 2 ) ( x − 2 ) name the same function, but they’re different formulas. One is a rule that says square your number then subtract 4; the other says take the product of 2 greater than your number and 2 less than your number. Since they give the same results, they describe the same function. Functions on sets In the late 1800s functions expanded so that they could be defined on things other than real or complex numbers. Set theory allowed for a function f to have any set S as a domain and take values in any other (or the same) set T . In the 1900s the notation f : S → T was developed for that. In the 1900s set theory was used to actually define functions. Given any two sets S and T , there is a specific product set denoted S × T whose elements are ordered pairs ( x , y ) where x is an element of S and y is an element of T . Then a function can be defined as a subset F of S × T with the property that for each x in S , there is a unique ordered pair ( x , y ) in F . Things like functions The concept of function has changed over the centuries. It’s really not just one concept. There are other concepts that could also be called functions. Random variables, multi-valued functions, distributions, and combinators each share some of the properties mentioned above, but each concept is different.

Question: Can a finite universe have an infinite number of possible things?

Question: How do you determine whether a function is even, odd, or neither?
Answer: First the definitions. These are discussed in calculus and precalculus courses. A function f : R → R is said to be an even function when for all x , f ( − x ) = f ( x ) . It’s said to be an odd function when for all x , f ( − x ) = − f ( x ) . Most functions aren’t either ever or odd, but a lot of important functions are one or the other. Every even degree power of x like x 2 , x 4 , x 6 and so forth, is an even function. Every odd power of x , x , x 3 , x 5 and so forth, is an odd function. That’s why they’re called even and odd functions. Also, sine, tangent, cotangent, and cosecant are odd functions while cosine and secant are even functions. There’s only one function that’s both even and odd, and that’s the constantly zero function. If f ( − x ) = f ( x ) = − f ( x ) , then 2 f ( x ) = 0 , so f ( x ) = 0. If you have the graph of a function, you can visually see when it’s even or odd. The even functions have a mirror symmetry across the y-axis, while the odd functions have a 180° rotational symmetry about the origin. Even functions  x 2  and  cos x Odd functions  x 3  and  sin x One of the properties of these functions is that the sum of two or more functions of the same kind is another. That implies that a polynomial that only has even powers of x is an even function, while one that only has odd powers of x is an odd function. So 4 x 6 + 3 x 2 − 5 is an even function (note that the constant term is 5 x 0 and 0 is an even number). Also, 4 x 5 + 3 x 3 − 5 x is an odd function. A polynomial that has both even and odd powers of x won’t be either even or odd, such as x 3 + x 2 . Moreover, the sums can even be infinite, so if you have the power series for the function, you can tell if it’s even or odd. If only odd powers of x appear, then it’s an odd function. For example, sin x . sin x = x − 1 3 ! x 3 + 1 5 ! x 5 − 1 7 ! x 7 + 1 9 ! x 9 − ⋯ . Likewise if only even powers of x appear, then it’s an even function. cos x = 1 − 1 2 ! x 2 + 1 4 ! x 4 − 1 6 ! x 6 + 1 8 ! x 8 − ⋯ . But if the power series has at least one even power of x and one odd power, then it won’t be either even or odd.

Question: If x<y<0, is y/x<1 always true?
Answer: First, an example. Take x = − 3 and y = − 2. It’s true that − 3 < − 2 < 0. Also, ( − 2 ) / ( − 3 ) = 2 / 3 , and 2 / 3 < 1. So it’s true in that example. In fact, it’s true in general. Here’s a proof. So that we don’t have to think so much about negative numbers, let a = − x and b = − y . Both a and b are positive. Now x < y says − a < − b . That implies a > b . Since both a and b are positive, and a > b , therefore 1 / a < 1 / b . That implies b / a < 1. That says ( − y ) / ( − x ) < 1. But ( − y ) / ( − x ) = y / x , so y / x < 1.

Question: How can I prove if x>y>0 then 1/x<1/y?
Answer: Your proof will depend on what you already know about inequalities. The typical starting point are the axioms of positive numbers. Then a > b is defined as meaning a − b is positive. The given statements are x > y and y > 0. The first says x − y is positive, and the second says y is positive. It follows by the addition axiom that x is also positive. You want to prove 1 / x < 1 / y , that is, 1 / y − 1 / x is positive. That’s equivalent to saying ( x − y ) / ( x y ) is positive. You’re given that the numerator x − y is positive. Since both x and y are positive, by the multiplication axiom, therefore the denominator x y is positive. You would be done if you could just prove that the quotient of two positive numbers is positive. That’s not among the axioms, so that will have to be proved from them. Theorem. The quotient of two positive numbers is positive. Proof. Let a and b be positive. By trichotomy, their quotient a / b is either positive, zero, or negative. If you can prove that it’s not zero or negative, then the only case left is that it’s positive. Case a / b is zero. That implies a is zero, but a is positive, and by trichotomy, it can’t be both zero and positive. So this case doesn’t occur. Case a / b is negative. That means − ( a / b ) is positive. Since b is also positive, therefore by the multiplication axiom, − a is positive. But by trichotomy, not both a and − a are positive. So this case doesn’t occur. Since the other two cases are excluded, therefore a / b is positive. Q . E . D .

Question: If y varies inversely as x square, how does x vary with y?
Answer: Assuming x is positive, if y=\dfrac a{x^2}\tag*{} where a is a constant, then x=\dfrac b{\sqrt y}\tag*{} where b is the constant \sqrt a. That means that x is inversely proportional to the square root of y.

Question: Does there exist a group of order 72 such that the center has order 12?
Answer: Recall that the center Z ( G ) of a group G consists of all the elements of G which commute with every element of G . Z ( G ) = { z ∈ G ∣ ∀ x ∈ G , z x = x z } What can you say about the center Z ( G × H ) of the product G × H of two groups? Suppose ( z , w ) ∈ Z ( G × H ) . Then for all ( x , y ) ∈ G × H , ( z , w ) ( x , y ) = ( x , y ) ( z , w ) . That says ( z x , w y ) = ( x z , y w ) , so z x = x z and w y = y w . That means z ∈ Z ( G ) and w ∈ Z ( H ) . Conversely, z ∈ Z ( G ) and w ∈ Z ( H ) together imply ( z , w ) ∈ Z ( G × H ) . So, you can say Z ( G × H ) = Z ( G ) × Z ( H ) . Therefore the order of the center of the product of two groups is the product of the orders of the centers of the two groups, | Z ( G × H ) | = | Z ( G ) | | Z ( H ) | . To answer your question, there does exist a group of order 6 whose center has order 1, and there does exist a group of order 12 whose center has order 12. Since 6 times 12 is equal to 72, therefore there is a group of order 72 whose center has order 12.

Question: What is the exact difference between positive infinity and omega?
Answer: They’re used for different things. Omega, written ω , denotes a specfic ordinal number. Ordinal numbers were developed in the late 1800s by Georg Cantor (as well as cardinal numbers). The finite numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, and so forth are the first few ordinal numbers. The ordinal number ω is the first ordinal number that comes after them. It’s an infinite ordinal number. Following that come ω + 1 , ω + 2 , ω + 3 , and other sums of ω and finite ordinals. They’re all different. After all those comes ω + ω which is also written ω ⋅ 2. There are many more after that. The term “positive infinity”, written ∞ or + ∞ , has various different meanings when something greater than all real numbers is needed. It’s usually written ∞ . The extended real numbers ¯¯¯¯¯ R includes the usual real numbers R as well as two other symbols − ∞ and ∞ , where − ∞ is less than all real numbers, and ∞ is greater than all real numbers. The arithmetic operations can be partially extended to ¯¯¯¯¯ R . Any finite number plus ∞ is defined as ∞ . Note that’s not the same as addition on ordinal numbers since ω + 1 ≠ ω , but ∞ + 1 = ∞ . Some operations on ∞ are not defined including ∞ − ∞ , 0 × ∞ , and ∞ / ∞ . (Those are called Not a Number (NaN) in the IEEE 754 floating-point standard for computers.) Besides ∞ in the extended real numbers, it’s used elsewhere. In the extended complex numbers where there’s only one infinity and − ∞ = ∞ there, so it’s a different infinity. There are other concepts of infinity in mathematics as well. In the cardinal number theory developed by Cantor, the first infinite cardinal number is ℵ 0 . There are many larger infinite cardinal numbers, the next one being ℵ 1 . The various concepts of infinity in mathematics depend on their context and how they’re used.

Question: What happens if a virus mutates into bacteria?
Answer: That kind of mutation would be a major evolutionary step. The virus would have to develop a lot of abilities that it doesn’t have. Viruses are very diverse. Some are extremely bare with almost on abilities at all. Some are quite complicated. Some can be bigger than typical bacteria. Those are the giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota. These giant viruses are DNA viruses. They already have genes for DNA duplication, translation, and repair. The origin of giant viruses is not clear. Did they evolve from smaller viruses by picking up genes from their hosts, or did they come from more complicated organisms and lost characteristics and became more virus-like? In either case it’s conceivable that over a long period of time they could develop the abilities needed to be like bacteria. Life forms and near-life forms on Earth are complicated. Scientists didn’t even know about giant viruses until about 40 years ago. There’s still more to be discovered.
